title: Monitor quality control practices in a food-manufacturing environment

lessons.title: Quality and quality control
lessons.html:
What quality means in food manufacturing

Quality means that a product consistently meets its specification and the customer's expectations, and is safe. Quality control is the checking and testing done during production to make sure products meet the specification, and to stop products that do not.

Quality control and quality assurance

  • Quality control (QC) finds defects: inspecting, measuring, testing samples.
  • Quality assurance (QA) prevents defects: procedures, training, audits and systems such as HACCP.

Specifications

A product specification sets measurable standards, for example:

  • Mass of each pack, with a tolerance.
  • Temperature at packing and despatch.
  • Appearance: colour, fat trim, no bone fragments, no blood spots.
  • Packaging and labelling: correct label, date codes, seals intact.
  • Microbiological limits tested by the laboratory.

HACCP

HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) is a system for food safety. The team identifies hazards at each step, decides which steps are critical control points (CCPs) where control is essential, sets critical limits, monitors them, and takes corrective action when a limit is not met. In a meat plant, chilling temperature and metal detection are common CCPs.

Legislation and standards

Food manufacturers must meet the hygiene requirements under the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972, abattoirs under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, and grading standards under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 where they apply. Many customers also require certification to a recognised food safety standard.

Every worker has a part in quality.

Know the specification for your product.

lessons.title: Monitoring quality on the line
lessons.html:
The supervisor's monitoring role

What to monitor

AreaCheckTypical record
Raw materialsTemperature, condition and documents on receiptReceiving log
ProcessLine temperatures, times, trim standards, CCPsCCP monitoring sheet
ProductMass, appearance, labels, date codesQC check sheet
HygienePre-operational inspection, hand wash, PPEHygiene checklist
EquipmentThermometer and scale verification, metal detector test piecesVerification log

Sampling

It is not possible to check every item, so samples are taken at set intervals, for example 5 packs every hour. The sampling plan states how many, how often and what to do if a sample fails.

Example: pack mass

The specification is 500 g per pack. Five packs weigh 502, 498, 505, 496 and 499 g. The average is 2 500 ÷ 5 = 500 g. Check each individual pack against the allowed tolerance too, not only the average.

Metal detector checks

At set times, pass the test pieces through the detector. It must detect and reject each one. If it fails, stop the line, hold all product since the last good check, and call maintenance and QC.

Good recording

  • Record at the time of the check, in ink or in the system.
  • Record actual values, not just ticks.
  • Sign each entry. Supervisors review and sign the sheets daily.

Hand over records to the next shift.

Review results with the team at the end of each shift, and highlight any checks that were missed.

lessons.title: Non-conformance and improvement
lessons.html:
When product does not meet specification

Immediate corrective action

  1. Stop the cause if possible, for example adjust the scale, stop the line, correct the chiller.
  2. Hold affected product: mark it clearly "On hold" and separate it from good product.
  3. Record what was found, when, how much product is affected and what was done.
  4. Report to the QC manager or production manager.
  5. Decide with QC: release, rework, downgrade or destroy, according to procedure.

Finding the root cause

Ask "why" until the real cause is found. Example: labels show the wrong date. Why? The date on the printer was not changed. Why? There is no start-up check for the printer. Corrective action: add the printer date check to the start-up checklist and train operators.

Trends and improvement

  • Track non-conformances by type, line and shift.
  • Look for patterns, such as mass problems after a product change-over.
  • Discuss results at team meetings.
  • Check that corrective actions worked.

Customer complaints and recalls

Customer complaints are investigated using batch codes and production records. If unsafe product has left the plant, a recall may be needed. Traceability records make it possible to identify exactly which batches are affected.

People and quality

Quality is everyone's job. Train new workers on the specification, explain why each check matters, and encourage workers to report problems without fear.

Key points

  • Quality control finds defects; quality assurance prevents them.
  • HACCP identifies critical control points with critical limits that are monitored.
  • Follow the sampling plan and record actual values at the time of the check.
  • Stop, hold, record, report and decide when product does not meet specification.
  • Find the root cause and check that corrective actions work.
